body.text: In a recent podcast, India’s Chief Economic Adviser, V. Anantha Nageswaran, stated that the “era of MBA is over” and urged society to place greater value on vocational skills such as welding, plumbing, electrical work, and carpentry as drivers of future employability.

However, data from the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) paints a more complex picture. As of June 8, 2026, around 2.83 million candidates had enrolled in NSDC-supported skilling programmes, but only about half completed certification requirements and just 23 per cent secured placements. Similarly, a performance audit of the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India highlighted a mismatch between training provision and labour market demand, noting that skilling efforts were concentrated in sectors with limited employment opportunities and that placement rates were only 41 per cent.

If vocational skills are indeed central to future employability, why do training and employment outcomes remain weak despite significant investments in skilling? More importantly, if industrial jobs are available, why are many vocationally trained youths choosing alternative forms of work instead? What does this reveal about the alignment between young people’s aspirations, labour market demand, and India’s skilling ecosystem?

These were some of the questions we explored during visits to three Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) in the Delhi-NCR region—a government ITI, a private ITI managed by a global charitable organisation, and an industry-run private ITI. All three institutes are widely regarded as among the best in their category. They had Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) with several private companies that funded laboratories and equipment, provided training for trainers, and, in some cases, offered placements and paid on-the-job training opportunities for students.

While all three ITIs were affiliated with the National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET) and followed its prescribed curriculum and assessment framework, the administrators in the private ITIs noted that parts of the NCVET syllabus could be updated to better reflect current industrial practices. To address this gap, they supplemented the curriculum with additional training modules. One private ITI was engaged in manufacturing and supplying steam turbine engines for sugar mills across North India, allowing students to work directly with contemporary industrial tools and processes.

In the industry-run private ITI, the training shop floor and workshop were designed to closely replicate the company’s actual industrial environment. This enabled students to acquire practical competencies alongside theoretical knowledge, through infrastructure that mirrored real workplace conditions.

Across all three institutes, considerable effort was being made to prepare students for industrial employment. The expectation behind these investments was that better training and stronger industry linkages will improve labour market outcomes and facilitate the transition from training to industrial work.

Yet, despite these efforts, training quality alone did not appear to determine students’ future trajectories. While students expressed interest in their courses, administrators across all three institutes noted that many frequently declined industrial job offers and internships. The reasons for this ranged from starting salaries not matching up to their expectations and factories being located far from their homes to fixed schedules and physically demanding work, which further reduced the attractiveness of these opportunities.

Instead, delivery services, ride-hailing platforms, and other forms of gig work emerged as preferred alternatives. Such jobs were perceived as offering greater flexibility, more control over working hours, and, at times, higher short-term earnings than entry-level industrial positions. Contrary to expectations, many students did not see factory jobs as their preferred career destination. Although industrial employment may provide greater stability and clearer opportunities for long-term career progression, these advantages often appeared less compelling than the immediate benefits associated with gig work.

This points to a broader challenge for India’s skill development agenda. Over the past decade, vocational education has been positioned as a critical pillar supporting the country’s manufacturing ambitions. ITIs are expected to produce the technicians, electricians, fitters, machinists, and skilled workers required by industry, as also echoed by the Chief Economic Adviser. However, the assumption that vocational training will naturally translate into industrial employment does not always hold true in practice.
Can industrial careers be made more attractive?

Today’s students evaluate opportunities through a wider lens. Alongside salaries, factors such as commuting time, working conditions, flexibility, and autonomy have become increasingly important. Moreover, the economic context within which young people make career choices cannot be ignored. According to the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2019–20, if a person earned a minimum monthly salary of Rs. 25,000, she fell into the top 10 per cent of wage earners in India, underscoring the limited earnings of the vast majority of workers. In such a context, vocational training and skilling initiatives must not only equip youth with industry-relevant skills but also create pathways to better-paying and more attractive employment opportunities if they are to remain effective instruments of upward mobility.
The rapid expansion of the platform economy has introduced alternatives that compete directly with sectors traditionally dependent on vocational graduates.

If these patterns are visible in some of the best ITIs, the challenges may be even more pronounced elsewhere. This raises important questions for policymakers and vocational education providers: why are industrial careers not attractive enough to the youth? Can better working conditions and stronger career progression pathways be provided? How can apprenticeships and on-the-job training be designed for greater uptake? And how should vocational education respond to the growing appeal of flexible platform-based work? The answers will shape not only the future of ITIs but also the success of India’s broader employment and manufacturing strategy.
Protiva Kundu and Bhuvaneshwari Subramanian are researchers working at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP), New Delhi. The views expressed are personal.
